questions.stem: A hospital uses a radioactive tracer to image a patient's thyroid gland. The tracer is injected into the patient's bloodstream. Which type of radiation should the tracer emit?

options.text: Alpha, because it is the most ionising and gives the clearest image
Beta, because it is stopped by the skin
Gamma, because it can pass out of the body to be detected externally
Alpha, because it has the longest range in the body

questions.explanation: For medical tracers used inside the body, gamma emitters are chosen because gamma rays can penetrate tissue and escape the body to be detected by a camera outside. Alpha particles (A, D) would be stopped almost immediately by body tissue and could not be detected externally -- plus they would cause significant damage to surrounding cells due to high ionisation. Beta particles (B) have limited penetration and would also cause more damage than gamma rays.

questions.stem: Gamma radiation is used to sterilise surgical instruments. Why is gamma radiation suitable for this purpose?

options.text: It makes the instruments radioactive, which kills bacteria over time
It is highly penetrating and can kill bacteria on and inside sealed packaging without opening it
It is the least ionising, so it does not damage the instruments
It has a very short half-life, so the instruments are safe immediately

questions.explanation: Gamma radiation is highly penetrating, so it can pass through sealed packaging to kill bacteria and other microorganisms on the instruments inside. This means the instruments can be sterilised after being sealed in their packaging. The irradiation does not make the instruments radioactive (A) -- irradiation and contamination are different. While gamma is less ionising per unit distance than alpha (C), it still ionises enough to kill bacteria. The half-life of the gamma source is typically long (D), not short.

questions.stem: A smoke detector contains a source of alpha radiation. Why is alpha radiation used rather than beta or gamma?

options.text: Alpha is the safest type of radiation because it cannot penetrate the casing
Alpha ionises the air between two plates, creating a small current. Smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm
Alpha radiation can detect the temperature of smoke
Alpha particles are attracted to smoke particles by magnetic forces

questions.explanation: Alpha particles strongly ionise air molecules between two charged plates, creating a detectable current. When smoke enters, the smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation (which has a very short range), reducing ionisation and the current. The detector senses this drop in current and sounds the alarm. It is also true that alpha cannot penetrate the casing (making it safe), but option A does not explain why alpha is specifically chosen for smoke detection -- option B gives the full mechanism.

questions.stem: A medical tracer used for a scan has a half-life of 6 hours. Why would an isotope with a half-life of 10,000 years be unsuitable for this application?

options.text: It would decay too quickly to be useful during the scan
It would remain active in the patient's body for an unacceptably long time, causing prolonged radiation exposure
It would produce too much radiation for the detector to measure
Long half-life isotopes cannot emit gamma radiation

questions.explanation: A tracer with a half-life of 10,000 years would barely decay at all during the scan, meaning it would remain radioactive inside the patient for years, causing ongoing radiation exposure and health risks. A short half-life (like 6 hours) means the tracer is active long enough for the scan but decays to safe levels within a day or so. Option A is backwards -- the long half-life means it decays too slowly. Long half-life isotopes can emit gamma (D is wrong).

questions.stem: Beta radiation is used in paper mills to control the thickness of paper. A beta source is placed on one side of the paper and a detector on the other. If the paper becomes too thick, what happens to the count rate at the detector?

options.text: The count rate increases because thicker paper absorbs more beta particles
The count rate decreases because thicker paper absorbs more beta particles
The count rate stays the same regardless of paper thickness
The count rate increases because the beta source gets stronger

questions.explanation: When the paper is thicker, more beta particles are absorbed by the paper, so fewer reach the detector and the count rate falls. The system uses this decrease to signal that the rollers need adjusting to make the paper thinner. Beta is ideal because it is partially absorbed by paper (unlike gamma, which would pass straight through, or alpha, which would be completely stopped even by thin paper). The source activity does not change with paper thickness (D).
